doc.title: Hal Galper interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 27, 2022

title: 'Fake it, kid': sitting in with visiting tenor players
summary: On house band gigs with visiting tenors, he learned tunes by faking and following the changes; he says he has faked it for sixty years.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: So if you’re in a house band and let’s say any number of tenor players are coming into town, Johnny Griffin, anybody like that, and you’re on the bandstand and they call a tune and you don’t know it, what happens then?
All right. Do you hope that the bass player knows it?

That’s right, except on those gigs that were tenor, piano and drums. Those were — in those days I used to take my fake books with me to all the gigs because I didn’t know the tunes, but they would never give you a chance to turn the page to get it. They’d say, “Forget it, kid, fake it” you know. So after two or three choruses if there was someone else playing the changes I could learn the song you know. But basic “fake it, kid” was the words I heard the most when I was young. And frankly, that’s the process anyway.
I was going to ask if that’s a lost —
I’ve been faking it for 60 years. When I started you could tell I was faking it. Now I’ve gotten really good at it. You know? So you can’t tell. Sounds like I know what I’m doing.
